meta.name: learnkit-ruleset
meta.description: LearnKit — machine-readable rule set for designing/generating neuroinclusive coursework and instructional content for any subject. Each rule carries a scope (content|platform|pipeline), an evidence tier, an automatable flag, and a before/after/why example. src/audit-content.ts implements every rule where automatable=true and scope=content; src/audit-platform.ts covers the automatable platform rules.

tierLegend.strong: RCT, meta-analysis, or normative standards body
tierLegend.moderate: single study, mixed literature, or non-normative standards note
tierLegend.contested: genuine disagreement in the literature; adopt only with rationale + test plan
tierLegend.inference: reasoned extension of sources, not directly stated

scopeLegend.content: checkable against generated instructional content (lessons, objectives, questions, rubrics)
scopeLegend.platform: governs the delivery UI/design system; audited in the rendering layer, not content JSON
scopeLegend.pipeline: governs the generation process itself (gates, labeling); enforced procedurally

checkTypeLegend.llm: requires a model judgment (multi-model or human-backed per TEC-8)

prohibited.pattern: Match instruction to a self-reported learning style (visual/auditory/kinesthetic).
Prescribe OpenDyslexic/Dyslexie as a reading treatment.
Ship a single hard-coded high-contrast-only color scheme.
Optimize feedback for delivery speed as a primary driver.
Justify engagement mechanics with vague 'dopamine' claims.
Encode status by color or emoji alone.
Use a single LLM-as-judge as the sole quality gate.

rules.title: Two-dimensional Bloom's cell on every objective
rules.check: Reject any objective/learning-outcome missing a cognitive process AND a knowledge type.

examples.before: "1.1"  (a bare objective id, no text or Bloom cell)
examples.after: { "id": "1.1", "text": "Explain how a model learns parameters from data", "bloom": { "process": "Understand", "knowledge": "Conceptual" } }
examples.why: Bare ids can't be checked for rigor, alignment, or Bloom balance.

rules.title: Single measurable action verb per objective
rules.check: Flag learning-outcome bullets with >1 assessable verb (e.g. 'define and apply') or a non-measurable verb (understand/know/learn/appreciate/be aware).

examples.before: "Students will understand and apply Newton's second law."
examples.after: "…define Newton's second law" (Remember×Conceptual) + "…apply it to solve force problems" (Apply×Procedural)
examples.why: "understand" isn't measurable and two verbs make pass/fail ambiguous.

rules.title: Bloom's ordering is not a prerequisite chain
rules.check: Non-sequential skill ordering allowed with a written sequencing_rationale.

examples.before: Analyze-level objective placed before any Remember objective, no explanation.
examples.after: Same ordering, plus sequencing_rationale: "a discovery task motivates the formula students then memorize."
examples.why: Non-sequential ordering is fine when the rationale is documented.

rules.title: Learning-goal (mastery) framing, not performance-goal
rules.check: Flag objectives containing score/percentage targets.

examples.before: "Score at least 80% on the module quiz."
examples.after: "Explain the trade-offs between INT8 and FP16 quantization."
examples.why: Mastery framing lowers anxiety and tunnel-vision vs a score target.

rules.title: Mastery goals for novice/complex modules
rules.check: First module of a track sets no numeric first-attempt accuracy target.

examples.before: Module 1 goal: "Achieve 90% first-attempt accuracy."
examples.after: Module 1 goal: "Understand the core vocabulary of the AI software stack."
examples.why: Specific performance targets overload novices; reserve them for consolidation.

rules.title: Self-system + metacognitive objectives where motivation is a barrier
rules.check: Self-paced flag => >=1 self-system and >=1 metacognitive objective present.

examples.before: Self-paced course with only cognitive objectives.
examples.after: Add "Identify why this skill matters to your role" (self-system) + "Monitor your comprehension with the end-of-lesson checklist" (metacognitive).
examples.why: Self-paced learners need motivation and self-regulation supports.

rules.title: Backward-design alignment (objective coverage)
rules.check: Every objective has >=1 aligned lesson AND >=1 aligned assessment item; every assessment item references a real objective.

examples.before: A quiz item tagged to objective 3.4 that no lesson teaches.
examples.after: Every item references an objective that has ≥1 lesson and appears in a summative.
examples.why: Backward-design alignment: objectives ↔ activities ↔ assessment.

rules.title: Segmenting with learner-controlled units
rules.check: Flag lessons whose estimatedMinutes exceed the segmenting threshold as candidates to split.

examples.before: One continuous 90-minute lesson.
examples.after: Three ~25–30m segments with a learner-controlled continue-gate between each.
examples.why: Segmenting keeps working-memory load manageable.

rules.title: Pre-training vocabulary before term-dense lessons
rules.check: Lessons past the term-density threshold must contain a vocabulary/prerequisite/key-terms section.

examples.before: Lesson opens with "tensor parallelism, sharding, and KV cache" and no primer.
examples.after: Prepend a Key Terms table defining each before the explanation.
examples.why: Pre-training the vocabulary frees capacity for the core idea.

rules.title: Manage intrinsic vs extraneous load
rules.check: Presentation-caused load (split attention, redundant text) flagged independently of topic difficulty.

examples.before: Diagram with its legend in a separate column so the eye must jump back and forth.
examples.after: Labels integrated directly onto the diagram.
examples.why: Split-attention is extraneous load the designer controls.

rules.title: Worked-example-first for procedures, then fade
rules.check: Procedural modules present >=1 worked example before the first unsupported problem.

examples.before: "Here's the concept — now solve these 10 problems."
examples.after: One fully worked example → a completion problem → then independent practice; fade support as skill grows.
examples.why: Worked-example effect (g≈0.48); withdraw scaffolds as learners gain expertise.

rules.title: Persistent progress + resume
rules.check: Progress indicator + resume-where-I-left-off present.

examples.before: No progress indicator; a refresh loses the learner's place.
examples.after: Persistent progress bar + "resume where I left off."
examples.why: Working across segments shouldn't rely on memory.

rules.title: Dual coding: visual per abstract concept
rules.check: Concept-heavy lessons should contain >=1 relevant visual asset (image/diagram/table).

examples.before: Three paragraphs describing a data pipeline, no visual.
examples.after: Add a labeled pipeline diagram alongside the text.
examples.why: Dual coding: pairing words with a relevant visual aids learning.

rules.title: No learning-styles matching
rules.check: Reject content that keys presentation on a self-reported learning style.

examples.before: "Pick your learning style to get a video or a text version."
examples.after: Everyone receives the diagram + text + narration.
examples.why: Matching to a self-reported style does not improve outcomes (Pashler 2008).

rules.title: Coherence + signaling
rules.check: Instructional pages use heading/signal structure; flag decorative-only media.

examples.before: A decorative robot-with-sparkles hero image on the lesson page.
examples.after: Remove the decoration; add section headings and arrows that signal the real diagram's structure.
examples.why: Coherence (cut extraneous) + signaling (cue structure).

rules.title: Temporal + spatial contiguity
rules.check: Captions/labels co-timed and co-located with their graphic.

examples.before: A figure on one screen, its caption revealed on the next.
examples.after: Caption sits beside the figure; in video, narration is co-timed with the graphic.
examples.why: Spatial + temporal contiguity reduce integration load.

rules.title: Modality + redundancy
rules.check: No simultaneous identical narration + full on-screen text over a graphic.

examples.before: Narration reads the on-screen bullet text word-for-word over a graphic.
examples.after: Graphic + narration; on-screen text trimmed to keywords only.
examples.why: Redundant identical text + narration splits the visual channel.

rules.title: Spacing: revisit each concept after >=1 day
rules.check: Each objective/concept has >=2 practice touchpoints across different lessons (proxy for distributed sessions).

examples.before: All cuDF practice lives only in Lesson 3.
examples.after: cuDF is revisited with practice in Lessons 5 and 8, ≥1 day apart.
examples.why: Distributed practice beats massing for durable retention.

rules.title: Retrieval follows instruction
rules.check: No assessment item references an objective/concept that no lesson teaches.

examples.before: A quiz asks about TensorRT before any lesson introduces it.
examples.after: Gate the item behind the lesson that teaches TensorRT.
examples.why: Retrieval should follow instruction, not test untaught material.

rules.title: Interleaving mixed problem types
rules.check: Practice sets past intro phase are not single-type blocks.

examples.before: Twenty identical derivative problems in a row.
examples.after: Interleave derivative, integral, and limit problems.
examples.why: Interleaving improves discrimination and transfer.

rules.title: Transfer-appropriate retrieval
rules.check: If the summative requires applied reasoning, practice includes applied (not recall-only) items.

examples.before: Definition flashcards preparing for an applied certification exam.
examples.after: Add scenario items ("what should the team do first?") that mirror the exam.
examples.why: Transfer-appropriate: match practice format to the criterion test.

rules.title: >=2 successful retrievals before retiring a card
rules.check: Spaced-repetition card-retire threshold >=2.

examples.before: A card is retired after one correct answer.
examples.after: Retire only after ≥2 spaced successful retrievals.
examples.why: One success doesn't establish durable memory.

rules.title: Explicit instruction before retrieval for low prior knowledge
rules.check: Prerequisite-gap flag => instruction precedes first retrieval.

examples.before: A novice is dropped into a cold retrieval quiz.
examples.after: Teach the concept explicitly, then retrieve.
examples.why: Low-prior-knowledge learners need instruction before retrieval.

rules.title: Surface desirable difficulty to learners
rules.check: Spaced/retrieval activities carry an explanatory rationale to the learner.

examples.before: A spaced quiz with no note; the learner feels it "isn't working" and reverts to re-reading.
examples.after: Add: "This feels harder because spacing strengthens long-term memory — that difficulty is the point."
examples.why: Learners misread effort as poor learning (r≈−0.36).

rules.title: Formative check before summative in each module
rules.check: Each module has >=1 FORMATIVE item positioned before any SUMMATIVE item; assessments carry a formative/summative label.

examples.before: Module ends with only a graded final exam.
examples.after: Add a low-stakes concept-check mid-module before the final.
examples.why: Formative practice before summative improves outcomes.

rules.title: Formative feedback: actionable, revisable, metacognitive
rules.check: Formative items expose criterion links + a revision opportunity + a reflection prompt.

examples.before: Feedback = "Score: 6/10."
examples.after: "Criterion 'evidence' unmet — cite a source for each claim. Revise before Friday's final. Rate your confidence 1–5."
examples.why: Actionable + revisable + metacognitive beats a bare score.

rules.title: Summative prioritizes application over recall
rules.check: Summative item set is not majority Remember/RECALL level; every item carries a cognitiveLevel.

examples.before: Summative is 80% recall-of-definitions and items carry no cognitiveLevel.
examples.after: Majority Apply/Analyze scenario items, each tagged with a cognitiveLevel.
examples.why: Summatives should favor application; tagging lets you verify the mix.

rules.title: Informational, not controlling, feedback
rules.check: Assessment items carry corrective/explanatory rationale per choice, not a bare score.

examples.before: explanation: "The correct answer is A."
examples.after: Per-choice: A "Correct: chlorophyll absorbs light energy to drive the reaction." B "Wrong: stomata exchange gases; they don't capture light." C "Wrong: mitochondria run respiration, not photosynthesis."
examples.why: Explaining why each distractor is wrong teaches; a bare verdict doesn't.

rules.title: Invest in feedback information quality, not speed
rules.check: Feedback objects carry specificity/elaboration fields; no rule enforces sub-second delivery.

examples.before: Requirement: "Feedback must appear in under 1 second."
examples.after: Invest in elaborated corrective content; let timing match level/domain (delayed is fine when it aids consolidation).
examples.why: Feedback timing is not a reliable main effect; quality is.

rules.title: Rubric descriptor mechanics
rules.check: Descriptors: no generic adjectives; impact not counts; parallel across levels; one page. (N/A if no rubrics present.)

examples.before: Criterion "Sources": good / excellent / poor.
examples.after: "Uses credible, peer-reviewed sources; citation errors do not distract from readability." (parallel wording across levels, one page)
examples.why: Observable, impact-based, parallel descriptors are gradeable.

rules.title: Rubric type matches task
rules.check: analytic (multi-skill) / holistic (quick/subjective) / single-point (formative).

examples.before: A single holistic score for a multi-skill capstone.
examples.after: An analytic rubric scoring each skill separately.
examples.why: Analytic fits uneven multi-skill work; holistic fits quick/subjective.

rules.title: Design for SDT needs (autonomy/competence/relatedness)
rules.check: Meaningful choices, informational feedback, achievable challenge, connection.

examples.before: A fixed linear path with scores as the only signal.
examples.after: Meaningful choices (autonomy) + informational feedback (competence) + cohort touchpoints (relatedness).
examples.why: SDT: satisfying the three needs sustains motivation.

rules.title: Overjustification guardrail
rules.check: No expected task-contingent tangible reward gates a high-interest activity.

examples.before: "Earn 500 points for finishing this project you already enjoy."
examples.after: Show mastery progress; drop the tangible task-contingent reward.
examples.why: Expected rewards on interesting tasks crowd out intrinsic motivation.

rules.title: Progress over social comparison
rules.check: No default public ranking; individual progress view present.

examples.before: A public leaderboard ranking every learner.
examples.after: A personal progress-over-time chart.
examples.why: Leaderboards demotivate those at the bottom.

rules.title: Goal-setting paired with planning/SRL support
rules.check: Goal-setting features ship with a planning/SRL scaffold.

examples.before: A one-off "set a goal" prompt on day 1.
examples.after: Goal + a weekly planning scaffold + self-regulated-learning check-ins.
examples.why: Goal prompts alone rarely produce lasting change.

rules.title: Gamification rewards are competence-informational
rules.check: Rewards express progress toward mastery, never controlling contingencies.

examples.before: Badges framed as "unlock to win."
examples.after: Badges framed as "you can now do X."
examples.why: Competence-informational rewards, not controlling contingencies.

rules.title: Celebration optional + reduced-motion aware
rules.check: Celebration honors prefers-reduced-motion and a user toggle.

examples.before: Auto confetti + sound on every interaction.
examples.after: Optional celebration that honors prefers-reduced-motion and a quiet-mode toggle.
examples.why: Surprise motion/sound can overwhelm; tie celebration to real accomplishment.

rules.title: No dyslexia-treatment fonts as default
rules.check: Font allowlist excludes dyslexia-'treatment' faces as defaults; content must not prescribe them.

examples.before: Default font set to OpenDyslexic "for dyslexic users."
examples.after: Well-spaced Arial/Verdana default; Atkinson Hyperlegible offered as an option.
examples.why: Dyslexia-specific fonts lack RCT support and can reduce fluency.

rules.title: Readability defaults + no ALL CAPS walls
rules.check: Flag ALL-CAPS runs (>=3 consecutive caps words) and wall-of-text paragraphs beyond the readability threshold in lesson bodies.

examples.before: A 600-word justified single paragraph.
examples.after: Short left-aligned paragraphs with headings and adjustable line spacing.
examples.why: Readability structure aids all readers, dyslexic ones especially.

rules.title: Accessible authentication (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8)
rules.check: Allow paste + autocomplete; no cognitive-test CAPTCHA without alternative.

examples.before: Login requires retyping the password, blocks paste, and gates on a text CAPTCHA.
examples.after: Allow paste + autocomplete; provide a non-cognitive auth alternative.
examples.why: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication.

rules.title: Redundant entry (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7)
rules.check: No field re-requests earlier-supplied data.

examples.before: Step 3 asks the learner to re-enter the email from step 1.
examples.after: Auto-fill or offer it as a selectable value.
examples.why: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry.

rules.title: >=3 palettes via a switcher on every page
rules.check: >=3 palette token sets; switcher present on every page.

examples.before: A single hard-coded high-contrast black-on-white theme.
examples.after: Default + low-stimulation + dark palettes, switchable from every page.
examples.why: Maximal contrast can be painful for autistic users; offer options.

rules.title: Breadcrumbs, bidirectional font sizing, stable nav
rules.check: Breadcrumb at all depths; font control decreases and increases; nav coordinates stable.

examples.before: No breadcrumbs; the menu moves position per page.
examples.after: Breadcrumbs at every depth, stable nav, and a font-size +/- control.
examples.why: Consistency and orientation reduce cognitive load.

rules.title: One-interaction stop on auto-content + resume
rules.check: Every auto-content element has a 1-step stop; resume state persisted.

examples.before: An auto-advancing carousel with no stop control.
examples.after: A one-click stop plus "resume where I left off."
examples.why: COGA: users must be able to stop auto-updating content.

rules.title: Never color/emoji-only status
rules.check: Every status token/indicator has a text equivalent; flag emoji-only status markers in content.

examples.before: A red dot 🔴 alone means "blocked."
examples.after: "Blocked" text + an icon + color.
examples.why: Never encode status by color/emoji alone (WCAG 1.4.1).

rules.title: Honor reduced-motion / forced-colors / contrast
rules.check: A reduced-motion path exists for every animation.

examples.before: Animations play regardless of the OS motion setting.
examples.after: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) collapses motion, plus an in-app control.
examples.why: Respects vestibular and attention needs.

rules.title: Literal, specific language for autistic learners
rules.check: Copy linter flags common idioms and ambiguous directional phrases in instructional text.

examples.before: "This next part should be a piece of cake."
examples.after: "This next task is short and has three steps."
examples.why: Literal, specific language aids autistic learners.

rules.title: W3C COGA objective checklist per build
rules.check: COGA 8-point checklist attached to each course build.

examples.before: Ship a course build with no cognitive-accessibility review.
examples.after: Attach the 8-point W3C COGA checklist to the build.
examples.why: Systematic COGA coverage, not ad-hoc.

rules.title: Personalization = pacing/palette/type/difficulty, not modality-to-style
rules.check: Preference values validated against an allowlist; never inject arbitrary CSS.

examples.before: A preferences field injects arbitrary CSS supplied by the user.
examples.after: Preferences chosen from an allowlist (pacing, palette, type, density, difficulty), validated server-side.
examples.why: Safe personalization — and not modality-to-style matching.

rules.title: ARIA tabs pattern complete
rules.check: tablist/tab/tabpanel roles + paired ids.

examples.before: <div class="tab" onclick="…">
examples.after: role="tablist" > role="tab" (aria-selected, aria-controls) + role="tabpanel" (aria-labelledby).
examples.why: Assistive tech can't interpret click-wired divs.

rules.title: ARIA tabs keyboard wiring
rules.check: Arrow/Tab/Space-Enter; Up/Down only if vertical.

examples.before: Tabs are only mouse-clickable.
examples.after: Arrow Left/Right move between tabs; Enter/Space activates.
examples.why: Full keyboard operability per the APG.

rules.title: ARIA modal dialog pattern complete
rules.check: role/aria-modal/label/focus-trap/Escape/focus-restore/inert.

examples.before: A modal with no focus trap and no Escape handler.
examples.after: role="dialog" aria-modal, focus trap, Escape to close, focus restored to the invoker, background inert.
examples.why: Keyboard and screen-reader users must not escape into hidden content.

rules.title: Custom widgets implement full WAI-ARIA pattern
rules.check: Prefer native HTML; custom widget passes its full APG checklist.

examples.before: role="combobox" on a div, with nothing else implemented.
examples.after: The complete combobox pattern (focus, active-descendant, keys) — or a native <select>.
examples.why: A role attribute alone does not implement the pattern.

rules.title: Design tokens in DTCG format, single source
rules.check: Valid JSON *.tokens.json; token iff $value; name rules; $type present/inherited; no reference cycles.

examples.before: Brand color duplicated in CSS variables, designtokens.js, and Tailwind config.
examples.after: One .tokens.json ($value/$type) as the source; generate CSS/constants from it.
examples.why: Parallel token sources drift; a single DTCG source doesn't.

rules.title: cmi5 (not SCORM) for LMS interop
rules.check: Package protocol = cmi5; verbs from cmi5 vocabulary.

examples.before: A SCORM 1.2 package with no out-of-LMS tracking.
examples.after: A cmi5 package using controlled-vocabulary verbs (completed/passed/scored).
examples.why: cmi5/xAPI tracks experiences SCORM can't.

rules.title: >=2 checkpoints before ready
rules.check: (1) after options proposed, (2) after alignment checked.

examples.before: The LLM emits a final quiz in a single unchecked step.
examples.after: Propose options → objective-alignment check → commit (≥2 gates).
examples.why: Unchecked generation ships hallucinations and misalignment.

rules.title: No single-LLM-judge quality gate
rules.check: Multi-model panel OR >=1 non-LLM check.

examples.before: A single GPT judge approves generated content.
examples.after: A multi-model panel or ≥1 non-LLM check (human, or retrieval against a curriculum KB).
examples.why: Single LLM-as-judge has systematic bias.
